text:
@wedusport @JohanBruyneel @BTPCycling #SpencerMartin @vismaleaseabike @TeamEmiratesUAE @RBH_ProCycling @decathloncmacgm @LidlTrek @giroditalia #Giroditalia27 @VingegaardJonas @TamauPogi 
The episode (THE MOVE+ Nov 6 2026) centers on the just-announced 2027 Giro d’Italia route, speculation on who will ride it (especially Jonas Vingegaard), sprinters, Primoz Roglic’s unsigned status, EF Education staff/budget issues, and Spencer Martin’s proprietary 2026 team “Season Quality Index.”

Johan Bruyneel and Spencer Martin treat the Giro as the main topic; other items are shorter. Their discussion is largely informed speculation based on public route details, known rider calendars/preferences, and transfer-market noise. It has solid merit on the route’s character and structural issues (e.g., snow risk, compressed geography) but is more speculative on individual rider plans, as is typical for off-season cycling talk.

2027 Giro d’Italia Route:
The route was presented in Rome on Nov 3 2026. It starts May 8 in Trieste (Italy), includes a Stage 2 hop into Slovenia (Ljubljana to Koper), stays mostly in northern/central Italy (no deep South beyond roughly the Rome area, and no Piedmont/Liguria/Valle d’Aosta), features Dolomites/Alps stages, and finishes May 30 in Rome. Total distance is 3,419 km with 50,250 m of climbing.

Key features that Bruyneel and Martin highlighted:
Stage 16 (queen stage): double Mortirolo + Passo Gavia (Cima Coppi) then summit finish in Aprica (5,700 m climbing). Extremely hard.
Stage 20: Monte Zoncolan. Extremely steep.
Two individual time trials: Stage 7 uphill (Sulmona to Campo di Giove, 19–20 km) and Stage 15 flat (Monza to Milan).
Roughly six flatter/sprint-oriented stages, eight medium-mountain, five high-mountain; multiple hard summit finishes.
Only a few stages over 200 km.
Transitions are shorter than the typical longer transitions from the Giro's past.
In Grand Tour parlance, especially the Giro, “transition stages” are the longer, typically flatter or medium-difficulty stages that link the key climbing stages.
The Giro has long been known for these “never-ending” days—often 200–240+ km—particularly when the race started abroad and had to travel long distances into Italy, or when it ran the full length of the country from deep south to the Alps/Dolomites.
These stages wear riders down through pure volume even when they are not full mountain days.

For the 2027 Giro, Spencer Martin and Johan Bruyneel noted that this has changed:
Only three stages exceed 200 km (Stage 8 Trasacco–Napoli 219 km, Stage 10 Palombara Sabina–Norcia 218 km, and Stage 11 Gualdo Tadino–Scarperia 220 km).
Most other stages fall in the 150–195 km range.
The route starts in Italy (Trieste) with only a short hop into Slovenia, stays relatively compact in the north and central regions, and does not go deep into the south or the far northwest. That removes the long transfer legs that used to be necessary after foreign starts or big north–south traverses.

The result is a more compressed route overall: fewer pure “transfer” marathons and a higher density of meaningful stages relative to total distance. This is a noticeable shift from many recent Giros that featured more of those long transitional days.

Early stages have meaningful climbing (e.g., Stage 1 2,500 m, Stage 2 2,200 m).
Bruyneel mentioned the classic Giro weather caveat: high Alpine passes (Gavia, Mortirolo, etc.) often face snow closures or modifications.

Their take:
It is a hard climber’s race with real GC action possible even if Stage 16 is altered due to weather, because of the Zoncolan, other summits, and the uphill TT.
Shorter stages and the Italian start (with an immediate Slovenia detour) are noted as deviations from recent foreign-start norms.
Elevation total is roughly normal for a Giro (comparable to recent editions at 45–52k m). They correctly note that total elevation is less decisive than how the climbing is distributed and how riders race it. Steep Italian climbs are unique and can create gaps even on non-marquee days.

Appraisal:
Accurate on the published route. The “built to lure Jonas” framing in the title is their speculation more than official intent with the Slovenia start being an obvious nod toward Pogacar. The snow-risk point is standard and has historical merit (Gavia has been affected before). Their stage classification and “still hard without Stage 16” assessment is a reasonable assumption.
Merit: high on description, solid on tactical implications.

Who Rides the 2027 Giro (and Who Wins):
This is the core debate. Bruyneel and Martin repeatedly stress that the race is defined by the starters, not the paper course.
Pogacar:
Almost certainly will not ride the Giro. Expected program is Tour + Worlds + Vuelta + Spring Classics. A Giro-Tour double after a full Classics campaign is viewed as unrealistic (they note he has done lighter Classics-to-Giro-Tour sequences before, but the full Flanders/Roubaix load makes it different).
Jonas Vingegaard:
Open/maybe. They float the idea that, if free to choose, he might prefer races without Pogacar. Winning the Giro would add another Grand Tour but Bruyneel noted that ultimately his main remaining motivation is beating Pogacar at the Tour. They treat a Giro win as near-automatic if he starts against the expected field.

UAE options:
Isaac del Toro (maybe), João Almeida (probable yes), Adam Yates or others possible. Leadership is unclear.

Felix Gall:
Yes. Good fit (climbing, uphill TT). He is viewed as a podium threat or more if the biggest names stay away; new team dynamics are a mild question mark.

Others:
Richard Carapaz (Giro a perfect profile for him), Giulio Pellizzari and Davide Piganzoli (Giro), Jai Hindley (strong course for podium), Derek Gee / Egan Bernal / Michael Storer possible, Florian Lipowitz and Remco Evenepoel areTour-focused, Oscar Onley the Tour, Enric Mas Tour+Vuelta, Lenny Martinez the Tour, Juan Ayuso the Tour, Brandon McNulty likely the Tour (especially if Almeida or del Toro take on the Giro). Ben O’Connor possibly a Giro-Tour double.
Primoz Roglic depends on finding a team.

If the absolute top names (Pogacar, Jonas) stay away, they lean toward del Toro or Gall as favorites to win, with Gall looking strong on paper given the uphill TT and climbing.

Appraisal:
Logical and consistent with public knowledge as of early November 2026. Pogacar’s program comments align with widely reported preferences. Jonas’s Tour priority is also the consensus view; the “avoid Pogacar if possible” idea is speculative but not absurd given recent dynamics.
Gall and Carapaz as Giro candidates have clear sporting logic. 
UAE leadership is genuinely unsettled.
Predicted winner is pure speculation (as they acknowledge).
Merit: Good framework for the transfer/calendar puzzle; individual “yes/maybe/no” calls are educated guesses rather than confirmed plans.

Sprinters at the Giro:
Six official flat stages, but several “hilly” days with modest climbs (under 3,000 m and non-summit finishes) are doable for modern sprinters. They both note the Giro historically has the most sprint opportunities among the three Grand Tours.

Speculation on what Sprinters will go to the Giro and/or the Tour:
Lidl-Trek:
Jonathan Milan to Giro (with Gall for GC) and Mads Pedersen to the Tour is floated as maximizing points-jersey chances (Ciclamino + green).
Milan won a late Giro stage in 2026; Pedersen is viewed as more versatile for Tour hard stages/green.

Soudal Safety Jogger:
Paul Magnier looks ideal for Giro but has Tour interest. Tim Merlier is the pure sprinter on the team. Dual leadership or partial Giro + Tour is discussed as difficult but has been previously tried.
Other big names (Philipsen, etc.) depend on Tour stage count and team priorities.

Appraisal: Reasonable. The “under 3,000 m can be a sprint day” observation reflects how strong modern sprinters have become. Trek allocation logic (Milan Giro / Pedersen Tour) is coherent for points jerseys and stage hunting. Magnier’s dual interest is plausible.
Merit: solid tactical read; exact rosters remain unknown.

Primoz Roglic’s 2027 Situation:
Still unsigned as of the recording in an unusually quiet market. They list closed or unlikely doors (Visma has said no, Tudor has said no or is cold, Pinarello-Q36.5 out, Unibet Rose Rockets and Lotto-Intermarché viewed skeptically).
Remaining possibilities include NSN (roster space, could write a bigger check), Bahrain Victorious (Slovenian connection via management/riders, Factor bike deal), or others.
TotalEnergies is dismissed (budget, French ProTeam identity).

Retirement rumors exist but they doubt he is done (Martin “still has tread on the tires”).

Appraisal: Matches contemporaneous reporting (Visma out, Pinarello talks collapsed, Lotto offer rejected, options narrowing, retirement talk circulating). Their shortlist is realistic given salary and roster constraints. Merit: high on the uncertainty; specific team guesses are speculative but grounded.

Other Team and Industry Notes:
EF Education:
Significant budget cut (publicly 15 %, hosts say larger).
EF lost riders (e.g., Carapaz) and key staff (Charly Wegelius to Tudor; Matti Breschel leaving).
Matt White returning from Movistar is viewed as a logical late-window fix because he knows the organization. They see this as a pattern of struggling to retain top talent.

TotalEnergies: Losing title sponsor, very thin roster (few riders under contract), always receives Tour invites as a French ProTeam. High ROI for a modest budget if they can stay competitive enough to be visible; risk of becoming invisible.
The name of TotalEnergies’ new title sponsor has not been publicly announced yet
As of November 6, 2026, multiple French reports (including Ouest-France and L’Équipe) state that team managers Jean-René Bernaudeau and Stéphane Heulot have reached an agreement with a new title sponsor for a three-year deal covering 2027–2029.
This replaces TotalEnergies, which ends its title sponsorship after the 2026 season.
Key details from the reports:
The sponsor’s identity is still confidential and is expected to be revealed early next week (L’Équipe specifies Tuesday, November 10/11, at an event in Arcueil).
The deal is intended to keep the Vendée-based team (active since 2000 under various names including Bonjour, Bouygues Telecom, Europcar, and Direct Energie) operating at UCI ProTeam level.
Budget is reported in the €10–12 million range.
A separate three-year bike supply deal with Chinese brand Pardus (replacing Cube) was already announced in late October 2026.
Until the official announcement, the new sponsor remains unnamed.

Team performance (Spencer’s 2026 index):
From the episode, Spencer describes an index he created as a composite that includes:
Wins (with bigger/more important wins weighted more heavily)
Podiums
Top-10s
UCI points
Visma is second overall in his index (with 27 WorldTour wins). Red Bull is third despite only 7 WorldTour wins, because they “scored a crap ton of UCI points.” He explicitly notes that Red Bull is second in the actual UCI team rankings for the year, ahead of Visma who is third. 
UAE dominant (40 WorldTour wins, roughly triple the second-place score).
Visma second (27 WT wins).
Red Bull third (only 7 WT wins but high in points).
Then Decathlon, Lidl-Trek, etc.
Picnic-PostNL near zero points (unbelievably dismal season; WorldTour viability questioned).
Movistar only two WT wins (both Enric Mas-related). 

Early announcement of full Tour teams (Visma style) is questioned:
Johan Bruyneel announced his Tour de France rosters in mid-to-late June, typically 1–3 weeks before the race (which usually started in early July).This was the normal practice during his years managing US Postal / Discovery Channel, Astana, and RadioShack.
Examples include:
2006 (Discovery Channel, post-Armstrong): Named the roster around June 16–17.
2007 (Discovery Channel, with Contador/Leipheimer): Announced around June 26–27.
2009 (Astana, Armstrong + Contador): Announced around June 25.
2010 (RadioShack): Presented the roster around June 22.
2011 (RadioShack): Still finalizing selections around June 20, with some riders locked in earlier and others still open (he even asked for fan input on the remaining spots).

Bruyneel did not announce the full 8- or 9-rider Tour squad months in advance or before the season. The selection was kept relatively flexible until spring form, results, and injuries clarified the picture. This matches the point he makes in the recent podcast questioning the modern trend (e.g., Visma-style early full-team announcements) because things change and it can demotivate riders left off the list.
In short, Bruyneel followed the traditional late-June timing that was standard for top teams in his era and questions why teams such as Visma announce their teams early.

Martin noted that specialized training camps are a counter-argument where the picked early riders for the TdF learn to gel well as a cohesive Tour team.

Appraisal:
EF budget and staff moves are publicly discussed realities.
TotalEnergies’ structural advantages (Tour invite + low budget) are long-standing.
Spencer’s ranking is proprietary (his own design) and therefore not independently verifiable here, but the directional results he states (UAE dominance, Picnic collapse, Visma strong on wins) align with known 2026 outcomes.
The early-team-announcement critique is a fair managerial observation from Bruyneel.
Merit: high on the news items; the index ranking is a useful internal framing.

Overall Assessment:
The conversation is typical high-quality off-season analysis, accurate on the freshly published Giro route, realistic about snow risk and stage character, and logically structured around “riders make the race.” Speculation on calendars and Roglic is appropriately hedged.
Biases are mild (Spencer’s American analytical lens, Johan’s managerial experience). Neither pushes a strong agenda. Claims that can be checked against the route presentation and transfer reporting hold up. The main limitation is the inherent uncertainty of November plans, exactly as they note.
The episode is a useful, grounded overview in a relatively quiet period, rather than definitive predictions.

text:
RESOLUTE

•The courage to continue.

Elon Musk’s journey with SpaceX offers a powerful example of what persistence can achieve. When the company began developing reusable rockets, landing a rocket booster and bringing it safely back to Earth was an extraordinarily difficult challenge.

The early attempts did not succeed. Rockets were lost, lessons were learned, and the work continued. Eventually, SpaceX achieved a successful landing, proving that a difficult goal could become possible through patience, learning, and determination.
The significance is not simply the landing itself. It is the willingness to continue working toward a difficult mission after failure.

Great missions are rarely completed in a single attempt. Sometimes the path forward is built from every mistake, every correction, and every decision to try again.

"The lesson is simple: when the mission has meaning, failure does not have to be the final chapter."

text:
Ty Jerome makes WAY too much sense for Boston…he makes $9M right now & the C’s have a trade exception, so $$ here doesn’t matter.

Also, Derrick makes $32M & is 32. There’s no chance White would be involved in a trade to a rebuilding team…in fact, Jerome is the kind of player that White works perfectly with (as we saw with Jrue Holiday).

White hasn’t been the same since.

But it should be CLEAR Memphis will want young assets, and Boston has plenty: Walsh, Hugo, Baylor, Cenac Jr., Dillon Mitchell, Williams + multiple 1st-round picks.

My preferred (and hypothetical) offers:

1. Walsh (22, makes $5M per year over the next 3) + Baylor (26, makes $3M & has a team option for $4M after this year) + the 1st-round LA pick (Lottery picks between 1-14 make $4.3M & $12.2M) AND TBH…this 2027 Draft Class ain’t lookin special at all!

That’s already $13M + right there (the C’s would only take on an additional $1M for the rest of this season…and I doubt Jerome gets a deal for more than $20M after this year — which I think would be a great deal for 3 years).

2. Hugo (20, makes $2.9M now, $3M in 27, & $5M in 28) + one of Boston’s own 1st-round picks & maybe a 2nd-rounder or two.

Personally, I’d rather hold onto Hugo…I prefer hypothetical #1…but Hugo would be a perfect fit for a rebuilding Grizzlies team….

Then again, if Mazzula isn’t going to give Hugo legit minutes, then do him a favor and let him develop somewhere that can use him. Walsh/Baylor take his minutes, and no signs of that changing anytime soon.

But to be clear, that would be my second option! Losing Hugo, but keeping the LA pick.

Walsh & Baylor + the LA lottery pick does it for me!

That deal does A LOT that I like:

C’s get Ty Jerome, a legit point guard.
It opens up minutes for Hugo…
It wouldn’t affect the salary cap.
It would put a dent $$$-wise to help extend Ty Jerome, so fuck that LA pick! Haha
Pressure off White & Pritchard.
More getting in the paint = more open shots for Mazzula Ball.

That’s my case for Ty Jerome:

Jerome is 29, in Tatum’s age range, and fills one of Boston’s biggest needs: another legitimate ball-handling playmaker who can take pressure off White/Pritchard and a guy who is a master at getting into the lane/penetrating defenses…which would be magic for Mazzula Ball. And a high-IQ player.

Regardless, it gives the C’s a dangerous backcourt again, and they are all set in the frontcourt as is.

The C’s have the assets. They can’t keep every young prospect and future pick while trying to maximize Tatum’s prime.

At some point, you have to turn assets into players who help you win. Jerome is exactly that type of move. #CelticsNation #Celtics

$FOCL Q3 2026 earnings: FocalTherics procedure volumes climb fast, but delayed machine sales cut its outlook

FocalTherics, a maker of robotic ultrasound machines for prostate surgery, saw hospital procedure volumes climb while delayed equipment purchases weighed on quarterly revenue. Sales grew 26% from a year ago and gross margin expanded nearly 5 percentage points on higher pricing, though operating losses widened. Chief executive Ryan Rhodes said three hospital machine deals slipped past the quarter's close, prompting the company to trim the top of its full-year sales plan. By our math, the updated plan points to fourth-quarter revenue growth slowing to about 21%.

• Revenue: $𝟗.𝟖𝐌 (+26% from a year ago)

FocalTherics makes Focal One, a robotic machine that uses high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) to destroy prostate tissue without invasive surgery. Each procedure requires a single-use disposable probe, so rising treatment volumes bring steady recurring sales even when hospital machine purchases stall. In the third quarter, US procedure volumes rose 32% from a year ago, and total treatment-driven revenue grew 24%.

That 32% volume gain slowed from 47% in the second quarter, because the company compared against 15% growth a year ago rather than the 4% to 5% base from the first half of 2025. Commercial insurance access also widened for men whose prostate cancer returns after radiation. Following a clinical guideline upgrade, Aetna, Cigna, Humana, United and several Blue Cross plans issued positive coverage policies over the past eight months, chief executive Ryan Rhodes said.

I was offered a job, celebrated with my family, and started planning how to spend my first paycheck. 
Then California's cannabis laws came back to bite me.

I'm 31, living in Sacramento, and had been unemployed for nearly three months. My savings were running low, rent was approaching, and I desperately needed a fresh start.
A few weeks ago, I interviewed for a warehouse and delivery driver position at a small logistics company. The owner, Richard, was friendly, and we immediately got along. We discussed my experience, salary, working hours, and responsibilities.
Before I left, he smiled and said, "I think you'd be a great fit here."
About 30 minutes later, he called and officially offered me the job.
I was over the moon. There was just one final requirement: a background check and drug test.

text:
WARNING: Before you buy Quiet Persuasion, I need you to promise me something…

Because once you’ve read it, here’s what you’ll be able to do:

‣ On page 140, you’ll discover how to make someone want something without ever asking him to. Use it on your wife, and she’ll walk into the jeweler’s convinced your Rolex was HER idea. Use it on a prospect, and he’ll pitch your offer to himself.

‣ On page 136, you’ll find out why the biggest obstacle to any sale is rarely the buyer… it’s the person sitting next to him. And how to take the wife, the business partner or the skeptical brother-in-law out of the equation without saying anything against them.

‣ On page 132, you’ll learn why the most persuasive thing you can do on a sales call is leave early. Done right, a man who said no on Monday will be chasing you by Thursday, wondering what he did wrong.

‣ On page 84, you’ll see why people stay in cults for 30 years, even when the leader is obviously lying to them. It has nothing to do with brainwashing. And the same mechanism explains why your best customers keep buying from you, even when a competitor is cheaper.

‣ On page 173, you’ll discover what a cake mix company did in the 1950s when housewives refused to buy their product. On paper, it made no sense. It worked anyway… and that same strange fix might be what’s missing from your offer.

‣ On page 174, you’ll learn why words like “revolutionary” and “breakthrough” can kill a sale… and the one quality your results should have instead, the one no copywriter wants to hear about.

‣ On page 151, you’ll learn how to give your customers a villain to hate. Done right, they’ll blame someone else for every problem they’ve ever had… and see you as the only person who can beat him.

‣ On page 114, you’ll find out why the most charismatic people you know have never worked on their charisma… and the one thing they understand that everyone else spends years trying to fake.

‣ On page 143, you’ll discover why people will live with a bad back for 20 years, but turn their life around after seeing one old photo of themselves. There’s a kind of pain stronger than physical pain, and one sentence is enough to wake it up.

‣ On page 186, you’ll learn how to make NOT buying feel more expensive than buying. It’s the same move a CEO used to hire a man who wasn’t even sure he wanted the job, in a single sentence, at the end of the interview.

‣ On page 204, you’ll find the 4 words a legendary copywriter wrote on an envelope to his publisher. They weren’t meant to sell anything. Yet they ended up on a mailing that nothing could beat for years.

‣ And on page 120, you’ll learn how to get total strangers to give you permission to tell them what to do. Not through authority, not through pressure… through one thing most persuaders never think of.

So here’s the promise.

If you’re thinking of starting a cult, a war, or a religion, please, I’m begging you, do not buy this book.

Otherwise, the link is in my bio.

text:
Two businesses can sell the exact same service to the exact same market and still need completely different YouTube strategies.

Why?

Because their business models are different.

One might sell a $500 product that customers can purchase immediately.

Another might sell a $20,000 implementation service that requires multiple conversations, stakeholder approval and a detailed evaluation process.

Both operate in the same niche.

Both have access to the same audience.

Both can create videos around the same problems.

But the content strategy that makes sense for one might be completely wrong for the other.

This is something business owners need to understand before investing heavily into YouTube.

Your content strategy shouldn't start with your niche. It should start with the economics and buying behaviour of your offer.

Here's how I'd approach it.

1. Understand the value of the customer before deciding what content to produce.

Start with your average customer value.

How much revenue does one customer generate?

Is it a one-time purchase?

Is it a monthly retainer?

Does the customer renew?

Are there opportunities for upsells or expansion?

These details matter because they influence how much time and money your business can reasonably invest in acquiring a customer.

Imagine two businesses.

Business A sells a $300 service.

Business B sells a $15,000 implementation package.

Business A might need a relatively high volume of customers and a simple conversion process.

Business B might be profitable with considerably fewer customers, provided the leads are qualified and the sales process converts.

Would you build their YouTube strategies identically?

You shouldn't.

Business A might benefit from broader educational content, product demonstrations and a frictionless purchase journey.

Business B might need deeper authority content, detailed case studies, implementation breakdowns and videos that help multiple decision-makers evaluate a substantial investment.

The economics change the strategy.

2. Understand the complexity of the buying decision.

Not every purchase requires the same amount of trust.

Someone buying a $50 product might need to understand what it does and whether it's worth the price.

Someone investing $30,000 into a business transformation needs considerably more certainty.

They might want to understand:

Whether the problem is significant enough to justify the investment.
Whether the provider understands their business.
Whether the proposed solution is appropriate.
What implementation involves.
What risks exist.
Whether the provider has relevant experience.
What happens if the expected outcome isn't achieved.

Your content needs to reflect the complexity of that decision.

For a simple purchase, a short demonstration might be enough to move someone forward.

For a complex service, you may need several detailed videos addressing different aspects of the buying decision.

This is why high-ticket businesses shouldn't blindly copy the content strategy of creators selling low-ticket products.

Their customers are making different decisions.

3. Understand your sales cycle before deciding how your videos should work together.

Let's say you sell a high-ticket B2B service.

A prospect discovers your channel today.

They watch a video about a problem affecting their business.

Then they watch a case study.

A week later, they watch your breakdown of how you approach implementation.

Two weeks later, they discuss your company internally.

Eventually, they book a call.

If you're only measuring the video that generated the enquiry, you're missing the wider journey.

Your channel might have influenced the prospect across several interactions.

Now compare that with a low-ticket product where someone can discover a video, watch a demonstration and purchase within ten minutes.

These are completely different buying journeys.

For a longer sales cycle, your channel needs to build familiarity, explain the problem, establish credibility and help people evaluate your solution over time.

For a shorter sales cycle, clarity, demonstrations, product value and frictionless conversion may matter more.

The content needs to match the speed and complexity of the purchase.

4. Build content around the financial consequences of the problem you solve.

This is where you can make your videos much more commercially relevant.

A business owner doesn't necessarily wake up wanting to watch another educational video.

They want to solve a problem that's affecting their business.

Your job is to understand the financial or operational consequences behind that problem.

For example, if you sell a customer acquisition service, don't only talk about generating more leads.

Explore:

How inconsistent lead flow affects revenue forecasting.
How high acquisition costs affect margins.
How poor lead quality wastes sales capacity.
How dependence on one acquisition channel creates risk.
How unpredictable demand makes hiring difficult.

You're connecting your expertise to the actual economics of running a business.

This also helps you identify topics that attract people with a genuine commercial reason to purchase.

5. Understand your margins and fulfilment capacity before scaling demand.

This is a mistake that doesn't get discussed enough.

A YouTube channel can successfully generate more enquiries while creating a bigger problem for the business.

Imagine your service has limited fulfilment capacity.

You publish content that starts attracting significantly more qualified prospects.

Sales increase.

But your delivery team cannot handle the additional workload.

Client experience starts deteriorating.

Deadlines slip.

Margins shrink because you need to hire quickly or rely on expensive contractors.

The channel is generating demand, but the business isn't operationally prepared to fulfil it.

Before scaling content production, understand:

How many additional customers you can serve.
What your current fulfilment capacity looks like.
Which resources become constrained first.
Whether additional customers improve or damage margins.
How long it takes to onboard new clients.
What hiring would be required to support growth.

Your YouTube strategy needs to support the business you can actually operate.

More demand isn't automatically better if you cannot fulfil it profitably.

6. Use your offer to determine which types of proof matter.

Different offers require different forms of confidence.

If you sell software, customers might want to see the product working.

If you sell consulting, they might want to understand your thinking and decision-making process.

If you sell an agency service, they might want to see how you execute, communicate and generate results.

If you sell a high-ticket implementation, they might need evidence that you can handle the complexity of their situation.

This should influence your case study strategy.

Don't just publish whatever results look impressive.

Publish evidence that addresses the risks your ideal customer is considering.

For example, if prospects are worried that an agency will disappear after receiving payment, create content showing your onboarding, reporting, communication and fulfilment process.

If prospects doubt whether your strategy works for their business model, show a relevant example and explain the conditions behind the result.

Proof needs to reduce the specific uncertainty preventing someone from buying.

7. Understand the lifetime value of the customer you're attracting.

A customer who purchases once and disappears is economically different from one who stays for three years, renews and purchases additional services.

This changes how much investment your business can justify in acquisition.

For example, a business with strong retention might be able to invest more in acquiring a customer because the relationship generates value over a longer period.

A business with low retention might need to prioritise acquisition efficiency and improve fulfilment before increasing its marketing spend.

Your content strategy should attract customers who are suitable for the long-term business model, not just people who are likely to make an initial purchase.

That means communicating expectations, implementation requirements and the type of customer relationship your business is designed to support.

8. Build your content strategy backwards from the purchase.

Here's the framework I'd use.

Before choosing video topics, answer these questions:

Offer economics
What is the average customer value?
What are the gross margins?
Is revenue recurring or transactional?
What is the potential lifetime value?

Buying behaviour
How long does someone take to purchase?
How many people influence the decision?
What information do they need?
What risks make them hesitate?

Fulfilment
How many customers can you currently serve?
What resources are required?
What happens when demand increases?
What makes a customer successful?

Content strategy
What problems attract the right buyers?
What beliefs need to change?
What proof do prospects need?
What videos support each stage of the buying journey?
What action should a qualified viewer take next?

Now your content strategy is connected to the actual business.

You're not just choosing topics because they have high search volume.

You're choosing topics based on the type of customer you need, the value of that customer and the decisions they need to make before purchasing.

The bigger picture:

YouTube strategy is not separate from business strategy.

Your offer determines what kind of customer you need.

Your economics determine how much you can invest in acquiring them.

Your sales process determines what they need to understand before buying.

Your fulfilment determines how much demand you can handle.

And your content needs to connect all of these pieces.

A business with a $100 product and a business with a $50,000 service should not be following the same content strategy just because they're in the same niche.

Don't build a YouTube channel around what your industry is posting. Build it around the economics of the business you're trying to grow.
